Present day, in a dystopian near future where the bubonic plague has returned. A remote, half-abandoned mountain village at dusk: cracked asphalt, rusting cars, a shuttered bar with a faded plastic sign, satellite dishes on crumbling houses, flickering sodium streetlights, windows sealed with plastic sheeting and tape, red crosses spray-painted on some doors. In the middle of the empty street walks the only person still fighting the plague: a plague doctor dressed in authentic seventeenth-century garb - a long waxed black coat, a wide-brimmed leather hat, a long-beaked leather mask with round glass eyepieces, leather gloves and a long wooden cane - completely out of place among the modern ruins. A few frightened villagers in modern clothes watch him from behind their windows. Wide shot: the doctor small but central, the street receding into fog.

First-person view of a plague doctor in seventeenth-century garb who has just entered a poor modern house in a remote village, present day, during a new outbreak of the plague. The room is a cramped kitchen with peeling floral wallpaper, a buzzing fluorescent tube light, a plastic tablecloth, an old television showing a muted emergency broadcast full of static, plastic chairs, and a door ajar onto a dark corridor. A family stands facing the doctor in tense silence: a gaunt father in a stained work jacket, a frightened mother in a cheap cardigan, a teenage daughter clutching a phone to her chest. First-person view of a barber in a remote mining village, present day, where time seems to have stopped in the last century: the barbershop looks untouched since the 1960s - a cracked leather barber chair, mint-green tiles, a big mirror with flaking silvering, glass jars of combs in blue disinfectant, a wooden radio, yellowed calendars, a bare bulb and grey light from a fogged window, a canary in a small cage on the shelf. The barber's own hands are in the foreground: one holds an open straight razor, the other rests on the customer's shoulder. In the chair, seen from behind, sits a coal miner just back from his shift; in the mirror his face and neck are still blackened with soot, and his reflection stares back at the barber with an unreadable, too-calm expression. Only one small detail betrays the present day: a modern smartphone lying on the counter among the old tools.

First-person view of a night-shift nurse in a military field hospital during a contemporary war, in an alternate present where technology stopped advancing around the 1940s: no electronics and no screens, only analog equipment, glass drip bottles, metal bed frames, enamel basins, a crank telephone, oil lamps and a few bare bulbs fed by a generator. The ward is a requisitioned school gymnasium with faded court lines on the floor and long rows of camp beds. Wounded soldiers in the uniforms of an unfamiliar army lie in the beds; many have heavily bandaged faces. The nurse's hand in the foreground holds a hand-cranked flashlight whose beam falls on one bandaged patient sitting upright in the dark, watching her through the gap in his bandages. A medicine cabinet stands open nearby.
